hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, dark visual forms—typically vertically oriented or compact silhouettes—set against a lighter, monochromatic background. The core activating features are defined by sharp dark-on-light contrast and often take the shape of vertical lines, crevices, or elongated bodies, such as deep fabric seams, vertical slit pupils, hanging cords, or the vertically aligned bodies of insects and arachnids. The neuron also activates for distinct, compact dark objects like liquid droplets, logos, or bird profiles, provided they are isolated against the lighter field. The activating features are consistently black, dark charcoal, or deep grey, while the background is a desaturated light grey, off-white, or white. The neuron is invariant to object category (responding to biological, textile, and mechanical subjects alike), surface texture, and minor lighting variations, as long as the strong tonal polarity is preserved. The feature typically occupies 10–50% of the image width and often extends vertically through 50–90% of the frame height, centered or slightly off-center.
